notes.summary: The capstone is where the path proves itself: you scope a project big enough to matter and small enough to finish, then build it with everything you've learned. OSSU's guidance: choose a problem you personally care about, define done precisely, and prefer shipping a working small thing over a stalled grand one.
notes.focus: Write the one-pager: problem, user, core feature, cut list, and 'done' test. If 'done' isn't testable, the project isn't scoped.

notes.summary: The design doc is a professional's superpower: architecture choices with rationale, the data model, the component map, and the risks — all before code. Your courses supply the checklists: security (6.858 threat model), data (6.830 schema), scaling (6.829/CS142), and the language choice by evidence, not fashion.
notes.focus: Write the two-page design doc and have one critical reader tear it apart before you build. Cheapest bug you'll ever fix — it hadn't been written yet.

lessons.title: Project Skeleton and Version Control Discipline

notes.summary: The professional skeleton: repository layout, README from day one, issue tracking, branch discipline, and CI running tests from the first commit. The Open Source Guides' best practices are the same habits paid teams enforce — adopted solo, they make your capstone feel like a product, not a homework folder.
notes.focus: Set up CI that runs a trivial test on push today. The discipline starts green and stays green — retro-fitting CI is a tax, starting it is free.

lessons.title: Vertical Slice: The First End-to-End Feature

notes.summary: Build the thinnest possible slice that touches every layer: one feature from UI to database to deployed. The walking skeleton de-risks the whole project — integration surprises surface in week one, not month three. Every later feature is then 'add depth,' never 'make it work at all.'
notes.focus: Ship the skeleton to production today, however humble. A deployed 'hello' beats a perfect localhost — momentum is the real feature.

lessons.title: Data Layer: Schema, Migrations, and Integrity

notes.summary: The data layer gets the most care because it's the hardest to change later: normalized schema, migration discipline (never edit, always migrate), constraints at the DB level, and indexes matched to real query paths. Your 6.830 training turns 'it works' into 'it survives data you didn't predict.'
notes.focus: Write the migration that would add a NOT NULL column to existing data — in a way that never locks or loses. That one migration exercises the whole discipline.

notes.summary: The service surface: resource-oriented endpoints, validation at the boundary, error responses with meaning, and pagination/limits from the start (never 'SELECT *'). Full Stack Ocean's Express routes are the pattern in production — measure twice, cut once on API design because clients depend on it.
notes.focus: Write the API's error contract (status codes + payload shapes) as documentation FIRST, then implement it. Contracts before code prevent client pain.

notes.summary: The dedicated security pass — not sprinkled in, but focused: OWASP's top-ten audit, authZ on every endpoint, secrets hygiene, dependency scanning, and the threat model from your design doc re-checked against the code as it actually is. Shipping this pass is what separates a portfolio from a liability.
notes.focus: Run the OWASP top ten against your capstone and write the fix for each finding in the issue tracker — including the 'not applicable because...' justifications.

notes.summary: Confidence engineering: unit tests for logic seams, integration tests for API behavior, a small E2E suite for user paths, and CI enforcing all of it on every push. Your 61B test-first habit, scaled to a system. Coverage is a map of what you trust, not a score to game.
notes.focus: Every bug you find gets a regression test before the fix. One rule, applied for the whole project, is how quality compounds.

notes.summary: Docs as the product's front door: a README that lands the value in three lines, setup that a stranger can run in five minutes, and architecture docs for the reader you'll be in six months. The discipline of writing docs exposes incoherence the same way writing tests exposes bugs.
notes.focus: Have a friend run ONLY your README's setup instructions. Every question they ask is a README bug — fix it before they ask twice.

notes.summary: The professional finishing pass: structured logs, real metrics (latency, errors, throughput), basic tracing of slow paths, and at least one measured optimization — profile first, optimize what the profile names, then prove it with numbers. 'It feels faster' is not a metric; before/after is.
notes.focus: Profile one slow endpoint, find the top consumer, optimize it, and commit the before/after numbers in the PR description. That commit is interview gold.

notes.summary: Ship, then watch: real users find the problems your tests never will. This lesson covers lightweight usability sessions (five users, focused tasks, silent observation), synthesizing feedback into prioritized fixes, and the iteration loop that separates products from demos. The Full Stack Ocean app you use daily improved through exactly this loop.
notes.focus: Run three five-minute sessions with people who have never seen the app. Watch in silence, note every hesitation, and fix the top two — then repeat once.

notes.summary: Halfway checkpoint: the core feature works in production with tests and docs, and the remaining plan is honest. The exercise: external review. Show it to a developer who hasn't seen it — their confusion and delight are the truest progress metrics you can get.
notes.focus: Cut the feature list by one third, right now. The discipline of subtraction is what separates shipped capstones from beautiful repos.

notes.summary: The release: final polish on the user path (errors, empty states, latency), the demo video or walkthrough, and the README that makes strangers care. Then step back: 8 terms, 24 courses, from counting problems to a shipped system. This project — visible, working, defended — is the proof the whole thing worked.
notes.focus: Record the three-minute demo: the problem in one sentence, the working path in two, and what you'd build next. Then close the issue tracker and take the screenshot — you're done.
